Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Thursday, 21 November 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 064)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health

MR MUSTON: Commissioner, this morning, we've got another
largish panel. Sitting in front of you, from your left to
right, Alfa D'Amato is back, Steven Carr, Neville Onley,
Matthew Daly, Joe Portelli and Sharon Smith.
THE COMMISSIONER: Can we treat Mr D'Amato as on his
former oath?
MR MUSTON: We can, but we are told that all of them wish
to give an oath.
THE COMMISSIONER: I'll leave it up to him.
<ALFAISTER DAVIS D'AMATO, on former oath: [10.00am]
<STEVEN CARR, sworn:
<NEVILLE ONLEY, sworn:
<MATTHEW DALY, sworn:
<JOE PORTELLI, sworn:
<SHARON SMITH, sworn:
MR MUSTON: I might ask each of you, perhaps excepting
you, Mr D'Amato, because you've already told us, but
everyone else, if you could just go down the table and give
your full name for the record and identify the role that
you hold within the ministry.
MR CARR: Thank you, Steven Carr. I'm the executive
director, system financial performance and deputy CFO at
the Ministry of Health.
MR ONLEY: Neville Onley, the executive director of
activity based management.
MR DALY: Matthew Daly, deputy secretary for system
sustainability and performance.
MR PORTELLI: Joe Portelli, executive director of the
system purchasing branch.
MS SMITH: Sharon Smith executive director of system
information and analytics branch.

MR MUSTON: Thank you.
Mr D'Amato, Mr Carr and Mr Onley, you have each
contributed to a joint statement dated 14 November 2024.
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Have you each had an opportunity to review
that before giving your evidence today?
MR CARR: Yes.
MR ONLEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Mr D'Amato has already told us --
MR D'AMATO: Yes.
MR MUSTON: -- but the rest of you remain satisfied, I
take it, that its contents are true and correct?
MR ONLEY: That's right.
MR CARR: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Likewise, Mr Daly, Mr Portelli and Ms Smith,
you have prepared for us a statement also dated 14 November
2024. You've had an opportunity to review it before coming
to give your evidence today and are satisfied that its
contents are true and correct?
MS SMITH: Yes
MR DALY: Yes.
MR PORTELLI: Yes.
MR MUSTON: And are satisfied that its contents are true
and correct?
MS SMITH: Yes.
MR MUSTON: That's exhibit M4, Commissioner.
Can I just start with a broad question about the way
in which the annual - let's start with LHDs, the annual LHD
budget is arrived at. Any of you who feels best equipped

to answer it, perhaps just talk us through, in a narrative
way, that process that is gone through by the ministry and
the LHDs when arriving at the ultimate point where the
service level agreements specify the budget.
MR DALY: I'm happy to start in terms of the process. It
is very much an overlapping one between the system
purchasing performance and --
MR MUSTON: Can I say in that respect, for the benefit of
all of you, you should treat this process as largely
conversational. For the benefit of these two people who
are taking down what is said, it's great if we could try
and speak as slowly as possible and leaning towards the
microphones. But, equally, don't feel that if a question
has been directed at one of you or one of you has given an
answer, that that precludes others from either contributing
further thoughts on the same topic or expanding on the same
topic or even asking one another questions along the way,
if there are things that you think would be usefully
fleshed out by asking one another questions about your
respective areas of endeavour. That is definitely
permissible.
With that interruption, Mr Daly, if you want to kick
us off?
MR DALY: Sure. Well, as I said, it's a process that
starts in about October of the financial year before,
that's largely led through Joe Portelli and Sharon Smith,
for their respective responsibilities, and firstly,
in October, it's about firstly reviewing the current year's
service agreements in terms of learnings to bring back to
inform any changes to the service agreements.
MR MUSTON: So when you talk about "learnings", what sort
of learnings are you seeking to obtain through that
process?
MR DALY: I'll let Joe give you some specific examples.
MR PORTELLI: Yes, basically any kind of learnings to do
with the process, the model, maybe inclusions that we
wanted to have for the current financial year but, with
timing, we couldn't, so we might want to hold them over to
the next financial year - so anything, any kind of either
process or model related --

MR MUSTON: Could you give us some examples of the sorts
of things - when you talk about process or model-related
things, what sorts of things are we talking about?
MR PORTELLI: So the timing of the meetings are really
important. If we don't have information at a certain point
in time there's no point having a meeting, so we will try
to shift that timeline and, you know, make sure that the
next year we've got more information to have more fulsome
discussions with the districts and networks. That's
a process example.
A model example might be that we want to include
a different purchasing adjuster into the model, and that is
predicated or that is calculated using historical data. So
if we implement it at a certain point in time, there is no
time frame in which the districts can actually act and
respond to that adjuster, which means they may get
a financial penalty or a financial reward, however minor,
but without any ability to change.
So we might decide to go, "Well, we've agreed and
discussed it with districts and networks. We think it's
a good idea, but we will implement that next year because
then they've got time to actually respond to the incentive
rather than just be hit with the consequence of it without
ability to respond."
MR MUSTON: So in terms of process, we're talking about
the process by which discussions lead ultimately to or the
process by which the service level agreements and budgets
are ultimately set. So the meeting that you refer to might
be if particular data about a service is not available to
the LHDs at a particular point in time, and that's been
revealed through the process, you might, for future service
level agreement discussions, adjust the timing of that
meeting?
MR PORTELLI: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: And in terms of the adjusters that you were
talking about, that's more substantive in terms of the
budget that LHDs might ultimately be receiving. What
information is informing you about, in that example, the
adjusters that may or may not be included.

MR PORTELLI: So in terms of the development of the
adjusters generally we go through that consultation
process. Depending on the type of feedback that we get and
the ability for us to reach all the different stakeholders
in the right time in the process, that might determine when
we can make a decision about whether to include that
adjuster. If that's the case, if it's too late in the
year, for example, we might decide to double the value of
a particular incentive for a particular model of care.
So one example is this year we decided that we thought
it would be a good idea to double the incentive for virtual
care, given the benefits. However, by the time we got to
the decision, because of various factors, there was no time
for the districts to change any models of care to respond
to that incentive, so instead we decided to delay it and
communicate it, and then that way, that kind of decision
will be factored in to this process in October where we go,
"Okay, well, what did we learn from the last process? What
are we going to do differently this year?"
MR MUSTON: Just teasing out that example, there's
a particular way in which virtual care is remunerated under
the agreement as a form of activity; is that right?
MS SMITH: Yes. So I'm happy to take that one. Virtual
care, if it's in scope of the activity that we deliver
across districts and networks and in scope of national
weighted activity units, it's already remunerated but we do
incentivise certain things in a relatively minor way, but
to provide, I guess, an additional payment to districts to
do those kinds of activities that we think have value and
that are going to derive longer-term value for the New
South Wales health system.
We use data that we have available already that
identifies where a service might be delivered by virtual
care but because it's historical, as Joe said, we need to
make sure that the district has time, so that when we do
look at the data just before the purchasing process begins
again, that if they wanted to increase the amount of
virtual care that they deliver, that that's evident in the
data, otherwise we're using data from before they knew that
we wanted to incentivise it.
MR MUSTON: I'm just trying to understand that, and we
will get into the details a little bit more, but why would

it not be equally advantageous to say, "From this point
forward we're going to incentivise the use of virtual care
for the delivery of activity", and then give districts
the benefit of that incentive and that uptick in income, to
the extent that they can achieve it during the immediate
12-month period, during which time they can then increase
their capacity, perhaps with the benefit of the additional
funding that they've got, to deliver more virtual care?
Why delay it?
MR PORTELLI: It's timing. So when we release the budget
we want to give certainty to the districts as much as
possible. We don't want shifting budgets within the year,
as much as possible, and then steps taken to try and reduce
supplementations throughout the year so districts have as
much certainty as possible, which means, with these
adjusters, we set them at the point of budget day and
that's based on the data that we have available. So for
the next 12 months, they will have adjusters based on their
performance in the last 12 months.
So having that time lag to say, "Right" - if we said
on budget day, "We're going to increase the virtual care
adjuster", the districts will be living with the
consequences of actions from 12 months prior, before they
knew that was going to happen.
So the positive adjuster is probably, you know, fine,
people get a windfall; but if it was a negative adjustor,
that's a material thing because they haven't had any
opportunity to change models of care or maybe change
behaviours in a way that would help them avoid that
penalty.
MS SMITH: I think it's important to note, though, that
the adjusters are fairly small in the general scheme of
things. So, for example, the virtual care adjuster
might have been a million dollars across the whole of the
17 districts and networks, and there are other ways in
which funding to support some of those initiatives does
flow to districts, but it's part of the purchasing model to
signal what is important to us as a system and the things
that we value and want districts to continue to do.
MR MUSTON: Accepting the distinction between positive and
negative adjusters, I'm still struggling - and it might be
me - to understand why withholding the benefit of

a positive adjuster in the immediate budget period is
something which is of benefit to the system.
MR PORTELLI: There's several considerations. One is
sometimes those adjusters are implemented at the same time,
so they are budget neutral overall. A decision around
including a positive adjuster, you know, when there's
a total bucket available, means that we will be taking that
from the top and not distributing that down.
Again, it comes to a decision on timing and I think
when we change adjusters, we don't want to change them one
on one; we try to change them in a bulk setting, so again
when they are - sometimes, again they're pretty small, so
when you try to increase one positive adjuster, you try to
have another one to modify behaviour as well, on the other
side, so it's budget neutral.
MR MUSTON: So the ultimate upshot of these adjusters,
year on year, would it be right to assume from that, might
not actually result in the LHD getting any more or
significantly more money?
MR PORTELLI: Sometimes they offset sometimes they don't
on a district-by-district level.
MR MUSTON: But across the system, they will offset?
MR PORTELLI: But across the system, it's budget neutral,
yes.
MR MUSTON: That being right, would it be right that the
risk of introducing the positive adjuster to enable LHDs to
get the benefit of it, but giving them a 12-month period to
acclimatise to the potential negative, would not be budget
neutral?
MR PORTELLI: Correct. And also I guess there's an equity
argument around the pool of money, how that is carved up.
If some districts could have taken more action earlier and
would have, they may have got more share of that particular
adjuster. So, again, it's probably fairer just to give
everyone the same amount of time to react, and people's
baselines can change within a 12-month period.
MR MUSTON: I think I distracted you, asking about the
learnings. So you told us that we go through the process

of reviewing learnings that can be obtained from past
budgetary negotiations. Where do we go from there, once we
have learned what we can learn?
MR DALY: I might get Joe to continue through, including
the overlap of finance and then the actual allocation of
budgets. I think that might be a bit more productive, if
that's okay.
MR PORTELLI: So after that point we hold a purchasing
workshop in December. In November we also talk with
finance as well around what some of the NPP proposals might
be. We share some modelling around population, ageing and
equity --
MR MUSTON: Pausing there, first thing, the workshop, is
that a workshop that's attended by all of the LHDs or are
we talking about separate workshops with each of them?
MR PORTELLI: No, we have a system-wide workshop, so all
the LHDs, pillars and all the statewide services are
included. We include relevant policy branches from the
Ministry of Health. Finance is obviously there and
presenting with us. It's sort of setting the scene for the
next budget process.
MR MUSTON: Then the next thing you told us about was
liaising with finance about NPPs that might be on the
horizon. Do we take it from that that the purpose of that
discussion is to work out what the existing envelope of
funding delivered by treasury is, probably get an
understanding of the extent to which it might be adjusted
by growth, but, equally, if there are new policy proposals
which have been put forward to treasury, getting some sense
of the likelihood of them being met with favour at treasury
and, if so, the consequences in terms of the overall
budgetary envelope that you have to distribute to the LHDs?
MR PORTELLI: Yes. I mean, I can talk you through --
MR D'AMATO: It's perhaps best if we step back a bit,
because that process is about one component of a budget, it
is not the whole budget.
So, for instance, as I described in my statement at
56, the overall budget is set on four key components. One
is the base, and I think it's fair to say that the

districts have an opportunity to adjust what the base looks
like, not to increase the base, but if there are service
configuration changes - and to think about one that has
occurred this year, for instance, where a hospital, in
Nepean Blue Mountains, used to be a third-party service, so
paid through our goods and services, it's now part of
our system, it means that they had to move the budget from
a goods and servicing to an employee related. So when we
then apply the next step, which is the escalation, related
to the budget allocated to salaries and wages, we have the
ability to increase the budget appropriately to reflect
that the wages may increase at a different rate for nurses
or other employees, for instance, just to give you an
example.
The third part of this, which is the part that is
associated with the work at the purchasing workshops and
the allocation, that component of the budget, is related to
the activity growth, which treasury describe to be this
1.5 per cent on the overall 4 per cent, that at the
treasury level is allocated to health.
Then the final part is the specific initiatives, and
this includes a number of things, but - and just reflecting
back to your comment about the NPPs. So there might be
NPPs being worked up at this time of year, around December,
where they may have activity included or may attract an
extra activity, as in extra NWAUs, and at that point, the
conversation with the purchasing team is to reflect, okay,
we might ask treasury for additional funding for this
particular initiative. If it is then reflected into
activity, that is included into the purchasing envelope.
Normally the policy area, so the branches in the
ministry, may have a say in respect to where and which area
of the system may receive this funding, and that's how it
is basically - and the sum of all of these is the budget.
MR CARR: The NPP process does provide, in the early
stages, a context for when we go around - and I attend with
Joe and Sharon to the different districts - a bit of
a context when we're talking to districts about what
they're saying they need, but also that helps us guide some
of those discussions. The NPP process early on might
change towards the end, but it does provide some context
for those discussions.

MR MUSTON: So when you say that the NPP process might
change towards the end, that's because a proposal put
forward to treasury might be accepted, might not be
accepted, might be accepted in part; is that right?
MR CARR: That's right.
MR MUSTON: Which, ultimately, the process that Mr D'Amato
has just talked us through, coupled with the outcome of any
NPPs, will form the budgetary envelope that's available
from treasury?
MR CARR: Yes.
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Mr D'Amato, when you were telling us a moment
ago about the base and the adjustment to the base on
account of, say, a hospital or a facility that has been
brought in-house, to use a simple term, is that
a discussion that's happening with treasury or are we
talking about a discussion that's happening at the district
level about their base?
MR D'AMATO: It's at the district level. And there is an
opportunity for the district to reflect changes
around February, so then we finalise the base
by March/April, and then we can start the calculation in
regards to what there is then to be allocated as what we
call "cost escalation".
MR MUSTON: The base that is made available to each of the
LHDs, is that informed at all, and, if so, to what extent,
by the base which is made available to the ministry in
general by treasury?
MR D'AMATO: Historically there is a relationship,
absolutely. Obviously, the bases inside the districts move
according, then, to decisions in regards to the purchasing
and some of the movements are more pronounced when there is
a new hospital, for instance.
MR MUSTON: We heard evidence on Monday from treasury and
Mr D'Amato about the somewhat mysterious history of the
base as identified by treasury. Can I ask in respect of
the base which is applied to each of the LHDs - it's
a figure which, subject to the sorts of adjustments that

Mr D'Amato has just told us about, is a historical figure;
would that be right?
MR PORTELLI: Yes.
MR D'AMATO: I think the challenge - sorry - to go back to
the base --
MR MUSTON: I think there was some nodding. If you want
to say "Yes", you have to say it out loud, so it gets onto
the transcript.
MR PORTELLI: I mean, from an activity point of view, yes,
but, like Alfa said, there is more to it.
MR D'AMATO: If I go back to when the bases were set, it
was when the area health services were split, basically.
They formed the base and at that point then we introduced
activity based funding through the NHRA. So from there on
we just started, where there was activity, new policy
proposals and the like.
MR MUSTON: Even at that point, was the historical
sequence that there were area health services which had
their own base of sorts?
MR D'AMATO: Yes, that's correct.
MR MUSTON: Albeit based on a different approach -
approach through a different funding lens?
MR D'AMATO: Yes.
MR MUSTON: LHDs were created by the carving up of those
area health services - that's correct?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: The funds that were traditionally made
available to those area health services, or the base that
existed within those area health services, needed to be
carved up and divided amongst the LHDs?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR PORTELLI: That's correct, yet.

MR MUSTON: So the base figures that the LHDs had, at
least at that point in time, bore some relationship to the
historical base which had been applied to the area health
services at some distant point in the past?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR ONLEY: So it formed the funding model, basically.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the extent to which the base which
has historically been applied to each of the LHDs reflects
the cost of meeting the particular health needs of the
community within those catchments, does anyone know when,
in the past, an assessment was made of that and whether or
not that was an adequate amount of money, at some point in
the past, to meet all of the health needs of the community
within either those area health services or more recently
the local health districts?
MR DALY: I could comment as a chief executive of two
previous area health services, when they were the big
beasts that they were, that there was far less local
influence and alteration; most of the activity was
routinely in place through traditional arrangements of VMO
appointments, both in terms of numbers and specialties and
sub-specialties, which is what drives your activity, and
then there would be, and was, programmatic influence from
the ministry or Department of Health, as it was at the
time, just as there is today, around particular areas -
could be mental health, could be drug and alcohol or health
prevention and promotion. But the influence or the
conscious decisions around changes to profile was less
active than certainly the devolved model that I've observed
since being back in the ministry for the last two and a
half years particularly.
MR MUSTON: Because we've heard evidence this week, and
again I'll invite any of you to disagree with this
proposition, but health is one of those areas where, "if
you build it, they will come", and with perfect efficiency
you could continue to spend money on standing up services
and there would be demand for those services within
communities.
MR DALY: Largely, yes.
MR MUSTON: And not only is it services that they would

like to have, it's services which, if you were able to fund
all of them, with good efficiency, would potentially be
providing good health outcomes for sections of those
communities?
MR DALY: Yes.
MR ONLEY: Yes.
MR MUSTON: But within the real world where we've got
a limited budgetary envelope which needs to be distributed
amongst the various priorities of government - health,
education, community services, transport, et cetera - there
is always going to be a confined portion of money which is
available to the health sector?
MR PORTELLI: Yes.
MR MUSTON: And that confined portion of money needs to be
used in a way which ideally delivers those services which
those running the health service think are, of the universe
of services that could be provided, those which are best
provided within the budgetary envelope - that is to say --
MR PORTELLI: Yes.
(Mr Onley and Mr Daly also nodded)
MR MUSTON: -- "We'll be given a bucket of money and we
will do with it what we think is the best we can do with
it", accepting it's not everything.
MR CARR: Trying to achieve the best value for money is,
I think, one of our objectives.
MR MUSTON: "Best value for money" in what sense?
MR CARR: Value in terms of patient outcomes; in terms of
looking at our - we have a range of KPIs in our service
agreement, which we try and achieve those, because they are
tied to our "Future Health" strategy, so we try and tie it
to those.
MR MUSTON: We might come back to them a little bit later.
Mr D'Amato?

MR D'AMATO: May I make a comment in regards to what you
were describing about having to work with a finite resource
and the way we allocate this?
I think it's important that we reflect on the approach
we have established in New South Wales in that decisions
around the budget allocation for new services or extra
activity is not a matter for finance. I think we
established this process where we're two divisions, two
clear distinct divisions, working collaboratively to then
determine how to distribute the new money, being the
activity.
I think it is important to reflect on that, because
activity based funding, ultimately, is a mechanism. It
doesn't drive the strategy. We just use the best possible
way to optimise efficiencies, to create the transparent
environment where there's benchmarking, when there is an
opportunity also to engage, probably also be more
accountable from both sides, be it the districts or the
ministry, but ultimately the decisions are separate to the
finance decision to the degree that there is an envelope
and that is always going to be the case, but how the
envelope is allocated, distributed, the mechanism and the
priorities are set by a different division. I think it's
important we reflect on that, because we are unique in
Australia in the way we implement activity based funding.
MR MUSTON: We might come back to that as well.
In terms of this discussion around the base, at some
point in the past when the area health services had their
base identified, it was presumably an amount of money which
reflected an assessment made at that point in time of the
best way, across the whole state, of distributing the
limited budgetary envelope that was available to deliver
the public health system, that confined suite of the
universe of services that we could be delivering, which we
decided was the public health system at that time.
MR DALY: Well, that was how the eight area health
services were formulated, which ironically was from the
28 previous area health services being amalgamated into the
large eight area health services, and it was literally
a matter of pulling the budget bases of those existing area
health services - sometimes two, sometimes three, sometimes
more, of those smaller area health services - in to create

the large one, with all the efficiencies that come from
moving from 28 delivery units to eight, and government had
a very clear agenda for what those savings should be
invested into.
MR MUSTON: So just taking it all the way back to that
point in time, accepting that the number or the figure that
reflected the total base spread across those 28 units might
have been an - I was going to say, "an arbitrary figure",
but a figure which was not necessarily informed by careful
assessment of precisely what amount of money was needed to
meet all of the health needs of the state.
MR DALY: Other than in programmatic areas, yes, it was
largely just an historical feature for those 28 --
MR D'AMATO: I think perhaps we also need to reflect back
then, at the area health service level, there was
a different funding model, which was the RDF, so that would
have influenced the way ultimately that the eight area
health services received their portion of the budget.
MR MUSTON: But the budget itself was, effectively,
a political figure, a figure that was determined as the
amount which would be applied to the delivery of health, as
compared with education, transport, the various other
competing demands on the budget, and in that day, the RDF
figure was the means by which the ministry used to, in
effect, divide it up amongst its geographic constituent
parts.
MR D'AMATO: Yes. Fundamentally, that's what it was.
MR MUSTON: And that historical approach to the funding
has come to inform, in a way, the way in which the money is
divided up amongst the LHDs, albeit instead of using that
formula as a currency, we're now using activity as
a currency?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct. The activity we've used then
from when we, call it, jumped off from the area health
services, the ABF has effectively allowed us to do the same
work but to distribute the new money across the system.
MR MUSTON: It might be useful, I'm reminded, if whichever
of you is best qualified could just give us the 100 words
or less description of what the RDF approach to funding

was?
THE COMMISSIONER: Can anyone remember?
MR DALY: From a practical perspective, the RDF, yes,
"resource distribution formula", which it stood for, was an
amalgam of a whole host of adjusters, if you like, in our
current parlance, reflecting all manner of socioeconomic
influences that will be within the community of that area
health service.
It's influence was fairly minor, but nonetheless, as
a true chief executive, I fought it because it was
disadvantageous to my area health service, which is what
chief executives do.
MR MUSTON: We were told that a few days ago.
MR DALY: But it actually made a marginal difference. But
health doesn't respond - and I think I used this term when
I last spoke to you - by revolution, it only responds
through evolution; and the RDF did, just as the purchasing
adjusters do, incremental changes around directing and
focusing financial resources to those areas of statistical
need that we can identify. So that's kind of the history
that I lived through for a number of years.
THE COMMISSIONER: I think in someone's submission they
have attached a press release from Mr Iemma, who was the
premier at the time, explaining the RDF with great pride,
only for it to disappear shortly thereafter, not through
his decision.
MR ONLEY: As I recall, it was reviewed every five years,
I think, so whatever the distribution pattern that it
derived was in for five years before another review
occurred. That's my recollection.
MR MUSTON: If we could go back to that historical time
when the 28 different constituent parts of the health
system were amalgamated into the area health services, we
were told - and you mentioned a moment ago - that the
efficiencies that could be generated through those larger
